heading: Compare money retained in a corporation with money reaching the owner
body:
A corporate tax rate is only one input in a C corporation decision. Owners also need to understand what happens when cash stays in the company, pays for business needs, reaches shareholders, or becomes part of a future sale. Build the comparison around the owner’s expected use of the business, rather than treating one annual rate as the complete outcome.

Use the same operating assumptions

Compare structures using the same revenue, operating costs, investment needs, and owner services. Show compensation, employer costs, retained funds, distributions, and projected tax in separate lines. A model that assumes a large salary under one alternative and no owner compensation under another may be comparing different businesses.

In a fictional company with $300,000 before owner compensation and tax, management plans to retain cash for a new location. That intention is different from a plan to distribute most cash for household spending. The adviser should model each scenario explicitly, including future cash extraction and an eventual exit. The retained amount is not automatically the owner’s personal after-tax wealth.

Bring a lifecycle question to the advisory meeting

State the expected holding period, likely need for outside investors, ownership changes, benefits, and possible sale structure. Ask which assumptions drive the result and which tax or legal costs would arise from changing an existing structure. A new company comparison may differ from converting a company with appreciated assets or accumulated tax attributes.

Use IRS business-structure guidance as a starting reference. The book is educational; a recommendation requires a coordinated company and shareholder analysis using current federal and state rules.
